title: Can and Could: Ability, Requests and Permission
summary: Use can for present ability or practical possibility and could for ability or possibility in the past. Ask for help, things or permission with can and could.
learningObjectives: Use can, cannot and can’t followed by a base verb to describe present ability or practical possibility.
Use could and couldn’t to describe what someone was able or unable to do in the past.
Make clear requests with Can you ...? and Could you ...?
Ask for something or request permission using Can I ...? or Could I ...?

explanation.heading: Can and can’t in the present
explanation.body: Use can + base verb when someone has a skill or when something is possible for them. Use cannot or can’t for a negative. Can does not change with he, she or it: say she can sing, not she cans sing. Never put to after can.
explanation.example: Our new neighbour can speak three languages.

explanation.heading: Could and couldn’t for the past
explanation.body: To talk about an ability or practical possibility in the past, use could + base verb. Use couldn’t when it was not possible. These forms refer to a past situation, so time words such as when I was younger and last night help to make the meaning clear.
explanation.example: At fourteen, I could swim across the small lake.

explanation.heading: Requests for another person’s help
explanation.body: Can you + base verb? asks a person to do something. Could you + base verb? is often a little more polite or less direct. In these requests, could is not necessarily about the past; it is a present request. Please can be added for politeness.
explanation.example: Could you move your bag, please?

explanation.heading: Asking for things and permission
explanation.body: Use Can I have ...? or Can I get ...? to ask someone to give you something. Use Can I ...? or Could I ...? to ask whether you may do an action. In a question, put can or could before the subject and follow it with a base verb.
explanation.example: Could I use the phone for a minute?

left.label: Present ability
left.note: Driving is a skill Mia has in the present.

right.label: Past inability
right.example: Mia couldn’t drive when she was sixteen.
right.note: At that earlier time, she did not have the ability.

comparisons.title: Asking someone to act or asking permission

left.label: Request to another person
left.example: Could you lend me a pencil?
left.note: The speaker asks the other person to do something.

right.label: Request for permission
right.note: The speaker asks whether they are allowed to do something.

examples.sentence: I can hear the music from the garden.
examples.note: Can describes what is possible for the speaker now.

examples.sentence: We couldn’t find the address yesterday.
Can you explain this word again, please?
examples.note: Can you introduces a request for help.

examples.sentence: Could I sit by the window?
examples.note: Could I introduces a polite request for permission.

commonMistakes.why: The verb after can remains in its base form.

commonMistakes.incorrect: I couldn’t to sleep last night.
commonMistakes.why: Do not use to between couldn’t and the main verb.
A request with Can you takes a base verb without to.
Can I is followed by a base verb, not an -ing form.

studyTips: Make two short sentences about the same skill: one with can now and one with could or couldn’t in the past.
Practise the pair Could you help me? and Could I use your phone? to notice who performs the action.
Remember that could in a polite request can refer to the present, even though could often describes a past ability.

exercises.prompt: Hugo has learned to read maps. He ___ read maps now, but he couldn’t when he was six.
exercises.feedback: Can read describes Hugo’s present ability; the base form read follows can.

exercises.prompt: Last year Leila ___ cycle long distances, but she cannot now because her bike is broken.
exercises.feedback: Could describes an ability that Leila had in the past.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is a correctly formed polite request for someone to close the window?
choices: Could I close the window, please?
Could you close the window, please?
Could you to close the window, please?
exercises.feedback: Could you asks the other person to close the window; the verb stays in its base form.

exercises.prompt: Which question asks permission to borrow someone’s charger?
choices: Could I borrow your charger, please?
Could you borrow your charger, please?
I can borrow your charger, please?
exercises.feedback: Could I asks for permission for the speaker to borrow the charger.

exercises.prompt: Complete with can: “My sister ___ swim across the pool now.”
acceptedAnswers: can
exercises.feedback: Can + base verb describes a present skill.

exercises.prompt: Complete with couldn’t: “Last winter, we ___ see the hills through the thick fog.”
acceptedAnswers: couldn’t
exercises.feedback: Couldn’t see describes something that was impossible at that past time.

exercises.prompt: Complete using Could: “___ you help me move this chair, please?”
acceptedAnswers: Could
exercises.feedback: Could you makes a polite request to another person.

exercises.prompt: Complete using Can: “___ I have a cup of tea, please?”
acceptedAnswers: Can
exercises.feedback: Can I have ...? is a natural way to request something.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: “Sam can plays chess very well.”
acceptedAnswers: Sam can play chess very well.
exercises.feedback: The verb after can is the base form play, not plays.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: “When I was seven, I can’t ride a bike.”
acceptedAnswers: When I was seven, I couldn’t ride a bike.
exercises.feedback: Couldn’t describes lack of ability at a past age.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: “Could you to check this address, please?”
acceptedAnswers: Could you check this address, please?
exercises.feedback: A request with Could you is followed directly by the base verb check.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: “Can I borrowing your pen for a minute?”
acceptedAnswers: Can I borrow your pen for a minute?
exercises.feedback: Can I + base verb is the correct form for requesting permission.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say that your brother has the ability to cook, using “can”.
acceptedAnswers: My brother can cook.
speakingExercises.feedback: Can cook describes a present ability.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say that you had the ability to ride a bicycle at the age of ten, using “could”.
acceptedAnswers: I could ride a bicycle when I was ten.
speakingExercises.feedback: Could ride describes a skill you had in the past.

speakingExercises.prompt: Politely ask someone to repeat the number. Begin with “Could you”.
acceptedAnswers: Could you repeat the number, please?
Could you repeat the number?
speakingExercises.feedback: Could you + base verb makes a polite request for help.

speakingExercises.prompt: Make a complete sentence from these cues to describe a present inability: My sister / cannot / join / us / today. Use cannot as one word.
acceptedAnswers: My sister cannot join us today.
speakingExercises.feedback: Cannot is followed by the base verb join to express present inability.

speakingExercises.prompt: Change “I can lift this box.” to say you were unable to do it last year. Use couldn’t and add “last year”.
acceptedAnswers: I couldn't lift this box last year.
speakingExercises.feedback: Couldn’t lift expresses inability in the past; lift remains in its base form.

speakingExercises.prompt: A visitor asks whether the lift is available. It is working now. Reply with one sentence beginning “You can” and using “use the lift now”.
acceptedAnswers: You can use the lift now.
speakingExercises.feedback: Can use expresses practical possibility in the present.

speakingExercises.prompt: A friend says, “Could I help you with the bags?” but wants to ask you to help them instead. Make the polite request beginning “Could you” and ending with “please”.
acceptedAnswers: Could you help me with the bags, please?
speakingExercises.feedback: Could you asks another person for help; could I offers help or asks permission for the speaker.

speakingExercises.prompt: You are on a phone call. Say two short sentences in this order: you can’t hear the other person clearly, and you politely ask them to speak more slowly. Begin “I can’t” and then “Could you”; finish the request with “please”.
acceptedAnswers: I can't hear you clearly. Could you speak more slowly, please?
speakingExercises.feedback: Can’t expresses present inability; Could you introduces a polite request.

listeningExercises.audioText: I could read music when I was nine.
listeningExercises.prompt: What could the speaker do at the age of nine?
listeningExercises.feedback: Could read music means the speaker had that skill at nine.

listeningExercises.audioText: Could you pass me the salt, please?
choices: Politely asking another person to pass something.
listeningExercises.feedback: Could you pass is a polite request directed to another person.

listeningExercises.audioText: I can see the sea from this window.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the one-word modal that describes present ability.
acceptedAnswers: can
listeningExercises.feedback: Can see describes what the speaker is able to see now.

listeningExercises.audioText: Marta couldn't read the small sign without her glasses yesterday.
listeningExercises.prompt: What was Marta unable to do?
choices: Understand the words on a sign.
Find her glasses in a shop.
Write a new sign for someone.
listeningExercises.feedback: Couldn’t read means Marta lacked the ability to read the sign without her glasses at that time.

listeningExercises.audioText: I can bring the spare chairs on Friday, but I can't come on Thursday.
listeningExercises.prompt: On which day is the speaker available to help?
listeningExercises.feedback: The speaker can bring the chairs on Friday but cannot come on Thursday.

listeningExercises.audioText: Could I leave my bike inside the building until lunch?
listeningExercises.prompt: Why is the person asking this question?
choices: To ask for help repairing a bicycle.
To request permission to leave something indoors.
To describe a bicycle they used to own.
listeningExercises.feedback: Could I asks whether the speaker is allowed to leave the bicycle inside.

listeningExercises.audioText: The lights were off, so Ben couldn't find his keys.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type only the negative modal expression immediately before “find”.
acceptedAnswers: couldn't
listeningExercises.feedback: Couldn’t find describes Ben’s inability to find his keys in the past.

listeningExercises.audioText: When I was six, I could already count to a hundred.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type only the one-word modal expressing the past ability.
acceptedAnswers: could
listeningExercises.feedback: Could expresses an ability the speaker had at the age of six.
